result: The UK Biobank study included 117,698 participants with 4,658 glaucoma cases (4.0%) and 113,040 controls (96.0%), with participants predominantly of European ancestry (85.8%).
evaluation: Reviewers acknowledged the large sample size as a strength, with one reviewer noting 'The huge sample size supports a powerful statistical analysis.' Another reviewer found it 'reassuring that the proportion of glaucoma cases (4%) is close to what would be expected in a population-based study of 40-69-year-olds of predominantly white ethnicity.' The sample characteristics were accepted without challenge.

result: Metabolites weakly predicted glaucoma (AUC=0.579) and offered marginal prediction improvement when added to models containing demographic and genetic data (p=0.002-0.004), with the best performance in Model 4 (AUC=0.806 with metabolites vs 0.801 without).
evaluation: Reviewers explicitly acknowledged this finding, with one stating 'The addition of NMR-derived metabolomic data to existing models containing clinical and genetic data was marginal.' The editor confirmed 'the evidence supporting the claims of the authors is solid.' The weak predictive value and marginal improvement were accepted as reported.

result: In the top PRS decile, elevated levels of glycolysis-related metabolites—lactate (p=8.8E-12), pyruvate (p=1.9E-10), and citrate (p=0.02)—were independently associated with reduced glaucoma prevalence.
evaluation: Reviewers affirmed this finding, with one summarizing 'Certain molecules in bioenergetic pathways (lactate, pyruvate and citrate) conferred protection.' Another noted 'This work provides additional evidence that glycolysis may play a role in the pathophysiology of glaucoma.' The statistical associations were not questioned.

result: The three resilience metabolites (lactate, pyruvate, citrate) combined significantly modified the PRS-glaucoma relationship (Pinteraction=0.011), with the highest metabolite levels in the highest PRS quartile corresponding to lower glaucoma prevalence (OR=0.71, 95% CI=0.64-0.80).
evaluation: Reviewers accepted this interaction finding, with one stating the authors 'report a "metabolomic signature" that is associated with a reduced risk (or "resilience") for developing glaucoma among individuals in the highest PRS decile (reduction of risk by an estimated 29%).' The editor confirmed 'the evidence supporting the claims of the authors is solid.'

result: Dietary pyruvate supplementation in Lmx1bV265D mice mitigated elevated intraocular pressure (p=0.002), anterior chamber deepening (p=4.4E-05), and optic nerve damage (p<0.0003).
evaluation: Reviewers affirmed the mouse model findings, with one stating 'They provide support for protection conferred by pyruvate in a murine model' and another noting 'Additional insights gained from a mouse model are valuable.' The protective effects of pyruvate were accepted without methodological concerns.

result: A significant interaction was found between glaucoma MRS (built from 168 metabolites) and PRS (Pinteraction=0.0012), with the combination of highest genetic and metabolic risk (PRS Q4, MRS Q4) yielding an OR of 25.1 (95% CI=18.8-34.1) compared to the reference group.
evaluation: Reviewers accepted this interaction analysis as part of the overall findings. The editor stated 'the evidence supporting the claims of the authors is solid' and reviewers noted 'Broadly, the conclusions are justified by the findings.' The MRS-PRS interaction was not specifically challenged.

result: The study has several acknowledged limitations: glaucoma ascertainment based on self-report and hospital records rather than clinical examination, a limited set of 168 plasma metabolites, focus on plasma rather than ocular metabolites, and cross-sectional design preventing causal inference.
evaluation: Reviewers raised significant concerns about these limitations. One stated 'Caution is warranted when examining and interpreting the results' due to self-reported glaucoma status and noted 'it is not uncommon for individuals in the highest PRS decile to have undiagnosed glaucoma.' Another reviewer emphasized 'selection bias and self-reporting are inescapable problems' and noted the 'correlation does not imply causation' issue. However, reviewers acknowledged the authors addressed these concerns, with one stating 'The authors have addressed the concerns of the reviewers and reported on the limitations of the study.'

result: Metabolites showed modestly improved predictive value for glaucoma among specific subgroups: White ethnicity (p<0.001), those aged 55 and older (p=0.002), and males (p=0.002).
evaluation: Reviewers did not challenge these subgroup findings. One reviewer asked 'Have the Authors explored how sensitive their predictions are to ethnicity?' but this was addressed in revisions. The final reviewer comment stated 'The authors have addressed all of my concerns,' indicating acceptance of the subgroup analyses.

result: Glaucoma cases were associated with male gender, older age, and higher intraocular pressure, among other clinical characteristics.
evaluation: Reviewers did not question these baseline demographic and clinical associations. These are standard epidemiological findings that were accepted as part of the study's descriptive statistics without comment.

result: The biological rationale for pyruvate's protective role is supported by literature showing that glycolysis end products are important energy sources for retinal ganglion cells, pyruvate has antioxidant properties, and previous studies have demonstrated neuroprotective effects in cell culture, animal models, and clinical trials.
evaluation: Reviewers affirmed this biological context, with one stating 'This work provides additional evidence that glycolysis may play a role in the pathophysiology of glaucoma' and noting 'Previous studies have demonstrated the existence of an inverse relationship between intraocular pressure and retinal pyruvate levels in animal models' and 'pyruvate supplementation is currently being explored for neuro-enhancement in patients with glaucoma.' The biological plausibility was accepted.

result: Literature supports the role of citrate and HDL-related metabolites in glaucoma, with lower plasma citrate levels found in glaucoma patients and HDL having antioxidant properties that can protect retinal ganglion cells.
evaluation: Reviewers did not challenge this literature-based contextualization. One reviewer raised a conceptual question about 'the distinction to be made between locally produced/available glycolysis end products and lipoproteins and those circulating in the blood,' but this was addressed in revisions and the reviewer confirmed 'The authors have addressed all of my concerns.'

result: The glaucoma PRS used was from a multi-trait GWAS analysis, constructed using 2,673 SNPs with MTAG p-values ≤0.001, and had a predictive ability with AUC of 0.68 (95% CI 0.67-0.70) in the Australian and New Zealand Registry of Advanced Glaucoma cohort.
evaluation: Reviewers accepted the PRS methodology without challenge. One noted 'The high-impact glaucoma-related GWAS publications referenced in support of the method suffer the same limitations' regarding UK Biobank data, but did not question the PRS construction itself. The methodology was considered rigorous.

result: A high-throughput NMR-based platform was used to measure 249 metabolic biomarkers (168 absolute levels and 81 ratio measures) in UK Biobank plasma samples.
evaluation: One reviewer raised concerns about sample quality, noting 'The optimal collection, transport and processing of the samples for NMR metabolite analysis is critical for accurate results' and that 'all UK Biobank blood samples had unintended dilution during the initial sample storage process' (5-10% dilution). However, the reviewer acknowledged that 'it is expected to have limited impact on most epidemiological analyses' per Julkunen et al. The methodology was accepted with caveats.

result: Common and rare variants in LMX1B are associated with glaucoma in humans, and mice with the Lmx1bV265D mutation develop IOP elevation and glaucoma, with severity depending on genetic background.
evaluation: Reviewers accepted the mouse model rationale and genetic basis without challenge. One stated 'Additional insights gained from a mouse model are valuable.' The use of this established glaucoma model was not questioned.

result: The prevalence of glaucoma in the UKBB sample (~4%) is similar to a directly performed disease burden estimate in a comparable United Kingdom sample (2.7%).
evaluation: One reviewer explicitly noted 'it is somewhat reassuring that the proportion of glaucoma cases (4%) is close to what would be expected in a population-based study of 40-69-year-olds of predominantly white ethnicity.' This validation of the prevalence rate was accepted positively.

result: The findings support that metabolite scores can identify individuals with high genetic risk who are less likely to develop glaucoma due to favorable metabolic profiles, and that pyruvate can act as a potent resilience factor when delivered orally.
evaluation: The editor affirmed 'the work offers insights for the design of protective therapeutic strategies for glaucoma.' Reviewers noted the 'Impact' includes that 'the protective effect of certain metabolites influences further research on novel therapeutic strategies.' The translational implications were accepted.
